home-remodeling.local_heading: Remodeling rules change at the causeway
intro_paragraphs: Key Biscayne's housing stock tells the island's whole story: 1950s Mackle-built concrete block houses in the village core, later ranches off Fernwood Road, and waterfront estates on Mashta Island, Harbor Point, and Cape Florida. Most were drawn for a different era of island life — closed kitchens, one modest bathroom, no laundry worth the name. Because buildable land on the Key ran out decades ago, owners who love their street tend to remodel deeply rather than move: full gut renovations, new layouts, structural openings, complete electrical and plumbing updates, and impact windows throughout.

Remodeling here runs through the Village of Key Biscayne's Building, Zoning and Planning Department, a separate jurisdiction from Miami-Dade with its own contractor registration, electronic plan review, and inspectors who know the island lot by lot. Two rules shape every major project. First, all of Miami-Dade sits in the High-Velocity Hurricane Zone, so windows, doors, and roofing need county-approved products. Second, much of the Key sits in a FEMA flood zone, where the substantial-improvement rule means a remodel valued near half your structure's worth triggers full flood-elevation compliance. We run that math before you commit, not after.

Twenty-plus years of building in South Florida and more than 150 finished remodels and additions, each one permitted and inspected, have made PGX Builders Group hard to surprise. On Key Biscayne that experience shows up as a fixed written scope before demolition, a supervisor on your site daily, and finish protection that treats your terrazzo and your neighbors' driveway with equal respect. One accountable team carries the project from estimate to warranty, and the paperwork that keeps a remodel legal is our problem, not yours.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to remodel my home in Key Biscayne?
faqs.a: Yes. The Village of Key Biscayne runs its own Building, Zoning and Planning Department, and it requires contractors to register with the Village before applying for permits. Structural changes, electrical, plumbing, mechanical, window replacement — all of it gets permitted and inspected. Unpermitted work has a way of surfacing at the worst time, usually during a sale or an insurance claim. PGX handles registration, submittals, and inspections as part of every project.

faqs.q: What is the FEMA 50 percent rule and will it affect my remodel?
faqs.a: Much of Key Biscayne sits in a FEMA flood zone, and the Village enforces the substantial-improvement rule: when the value of improvements approaches half the market value of the structure itself, the entire building must be brought into compliance with current flood-elevation standards. That can reshape a project's scope or budget dramatically, so we run the numbers with you before design gets far. Sometimes it changes the plan; it should never be a surprise.

faqs.q: How long does a whole-home remodel take on the island?
faqs.a: The honest answer depends on scope. Design and Village permitting typically take a few months for a major remodel, with construction running several more. Island logistics add real planning: one causeway on and off, and material deliveries scheduled so your street is not blocked for weeks. We build the timeline into the written scope and report progress regularly, so you always know where the project stands.

faqs.q: Should we remodel our 1950s Mackle house or tear it down and rebuild?
faqs.a: It depends on what you love about the house and what the flood math says. Many Mackle-era homes are solid concrete block worth keeping, and a deep remodel can deliver a modern home while preserving the scale of the street. But when the scope approaches the substantial-improvement threshold, a rebuild sometimes makes more sense. We give you a straight comparison — scope, numbers, tradeoffs — and we are comfortable either way, so the advice is not a sales pitch.

faqs.q: What does a high-end whole-home remodel cost in Key Biscayne?
faqs.a: There is no honest single number: a whole-home remodel spans a wide range depending on structural scope, systems, and finish level, and island projects carry real logistics costs. What we can promise is the shape of the number — a fixed written scope with allowances spelled out, so the price you sign is the price that governs. PGX is a high-end contractor, not the cheapest bid, and our clients hire us so the budget holds.

kitchen-remodeling.local_heading: Two kinds of Key Biscayne kitchens
intro_paragraphs: Key Biscayne cooks in two languages. In the village core and out toward Cape Florida, owners of 1950s and 60s block houses are taking down the wall that kept the kitchen hidden, adding islands, and rebuilding around custom cabinetry and serious ventilation. Meanwhile, in the towers — Key Colony, Ocean Club, Oceana — original condo kitchens from the 70s, 80s, and 90s are being gutted to the slab and rebuilt with stone counters, panel-ready appliances, and lighting that finally does the ocean view justice. Different buildings, same standard of work.

Either way, the permits run through the Village of Key Biscayne's Building, Zoning and Planning Department, which registers every contractor before it accepts an application. Condo work adds a second layer: association approval of plans, certificates of insurance, service-elevator reservations, and weekday work windows that we schedule around rather than argue with. Moving a sink, a range, or a panel means plumbing and electrical permits and inspections — the part of a kitchen remodel nobody photographs but every appraiser checks. We handle both layers and keep the building manager on a first-name basis.

PGX builds kitchens the way a licensed general contractor should: a fixed written scope with allowances spelled out, a daily supervisor who opens and closes the site, and floor-to-ceiling protection through the lobby, the elevator, and your hallway. Cabinetry is built to order, counters are templated after cabinets are set, and appliance relocations are engineered rather than improvised. After 20-plus years and more than 150 remodels across South Florida, we have learned that on Key Biscayne, discretion and a clean job site are as much a part of the finish schedule as the stone.

faqs.q: Can I remodel my kitchen in a Key Biscayne condo like Key Colony or Ocean Club?
faqs.a: Yes — condo kitchens across the island's towers get gutted and rebuilt all the time. The process adds an association layer: plan approval, certificates of insurance, contractor registration with the building, service-elevator reservations, and set work hours. We prepare the submittal package, coordinate with management, and schedule crews around the building's rules rather than against them. It takes some patience, and it is entirely routine when your contractor has done it before.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit just to replace kitchen cabinets?
faqs.a: A true like-for-like cabinet swap with no plumbing, electrical, or wall changes may not need one, but almost no real kitchen remodel stays that simple. Move a sink, relocate an outlet, add an island with power, or touch a wall, and you need permits and inspections through the Village of Key Biscayne. We tell you exactly which parts of your project trigger review during the first walk-through, before anything is ordered.

faqs.q: How long does a custom kitchen remodel take?
faqs.a: The schedule is usually driven by cabinetry, not construction. Custom cabinets carry lead times measured in weeks to months, so we finalize the design, order early, and time demolition so your kitchen is out of service for the shortest stretch possible. Site work typically runs several weeks for a full remodel; condo work windows can stretch that somewhat. You will have the sequence in writing before we open a single cabinet door.

faqs.q: Can you remove the wall between my kitchen and living room?
faqs.a: Usually, yes — and in Mackle-era block houses that wall is often structural, which means an engineered beam, a Village permit, and proper inspections rather than a sledgehammer and optimism. This is one of the most common moves on the island because the original floor plans kept kitchens sealed off from everything. Done right, it transforms the whole main floor. Done wrong, it becomes somebody else's expensive repair, so we only do it right.

faqs.q: What should I budget for a high-end kitchen in Key Biscayne?
faqs.a: Custom cabinetry, natural stone, and appliance relocation put island kitchens in a wide but predictable range; the biggest swings come from cabinet scope, slab selection, and how far plumbing and electrical move. Rather than quote a fantasy number, we scope your actual kitchen, price it line by line, and fix it in writing with allowances you control. Clients hire PGX for a number that holds, not the lowest opening offer.

intro_paragraphs: The original Key Biscayne house shipped with one bathroom, and it was not generous. Seventy years later, owners in the village core and Biscayne Key Estates are carving real primary suites out of bedroom wings, while waterfront homes on Mashta Island and Harbor Point get the full treatment: freestanding tubs, book-matched stone, showers with more plumbing than the original house had in total. In the condo towers, baths from the 70s and 80s are being gutted to the slab, where the tile is usually the youngest thing in the wall.

Bathroom work is plumbing and electrical work, which means permits and inspections through the Village of Key Biscayne's Building, Zoning and Planning Department — no exceptions for small footprints. In the towers, tying into a building riser takes association approval and a scheduled water shut-down for your stack, which we coordinate with management rather than spring on your neighbors. Florida's post-Surfside milestone-inspection era has made island boards rightly attentive to what happens inside walls and slabs, so our submittals arrive complete: drawings, insurance, licensing, and a schedule the building can hold us to.

This is the trade where PGX is least willing to negotiate. Every shower gets a full waterproofing assembly — pan, membrane, flood test — because on an island with this much humidity, a shortcut behind the tile becomes a demolition order in five years. A written scope fixes the fixtures, stone, and glass before we open a wall; a supervisor checks the site daily; and the same licensed team (Lic. CGC1539072) answers for the job from first sketch to warranty call. It is a small room. That is exactly why the details are the whole project.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for a bathroom remodel in Key Biscayne?
faqs.a: Yes. Bathroom remodels involve plumbing and electrical work, which the Village of Key Biscayne permits and inspects regardless of the room's size. Your contractor also has to be registered with the Village before applying. It adds a little process, and it is the reason a finished PGX bathroom comes with an inspection record instead of an open question when you refinance or sell.

faqs.q: Can you renovate a bathroom in one of the older condo towers?
faqs.a: Yes, and we do it with the building's cooperation rather than around it. Older Key Biscayne towers often have original branch valves and risers, so tying in new plumbing means association approval and a scheduled water shut-down for your stack. We coordinate the notice with management, replace what is worn at the connection while the wall is open, and follow the building's rules on hours, elevators, and protection without drama.

faqs.q: How do you keep a new bathroom from growing mold on an island this humid?
faqs.a: By treating waterproofing and ventilation as the project, not accessories to the tile. Every PGX shower gets a complete waterproofing assembly with a flood test before finishes go on, exhaust ventilation is sized and ducted properly, and we detail the transitions — niches, benches, curbs — where failures actually start. Key Biscayne humidity punishes shortcuts behind walls. Our answer is not a special product; it is refusing to skip steps nobody would see us skip.

faqs.q: How long does a primary bathroom remodel take?
faqs.a: A full gut of a primary bath generally runs several weeks of construction once materials are in hand, plus lead time for stone, fixtures, and custom glass — glass is templated after tile, so it always trails the finish work. Condo association work windows can add calendar time. We sequence orders before demolition so the room is torn up once, briefly, instead of twice, indefinitely.

faqs.q: What does a high-end bathroom remodel cost on the Key?
faqs.a: Bathrooms concentrate cost per square foot: stone, glass, plumbing fixtures, and waterproofing all live in a small footprint, and moving fixtures adds real plumbing scope. Ranges vary widely with finish level, so we would rather walk your actual bathroom and write a fixed scope than recite a number that fits nobody. home-additions.local_heading: Adding on where land ran out
intro_paragraphs: Nobody is making more Key Biscayne. The island built out decades ago, which is why families who outgrow a three-bedroom Mackle house near the Village Green rarely find a bigger one two streets over — they build up or build back instead. Second-story additions turn 1950s footprints into modern family homes; rear extensions push kitchens and family rooms toward the pool; garage conversions become in-law suites for the grandparents who visit in November and leave in May. On the waterfront streets of Smugglers Cove and Mashta Island, additions run larger and lean harder on engineering.

An addition on the Key answers to more reviewers than most Miami projects. The Village of Key Biscayne's Building, Zoning and Planning Department checks setbacks, lot coverage, and height before structure is even discussed. Because most of the island sits in a FEMA flood zone, new habitable space must meet base flood elevation requirements, and the substantial-improvement rule can pull the existing house into compliance if the project's value climbs near half the structure's worth. Add High-Velocity Hurricane Zone engineering — tie-beams, uplift connections, approved openings — and the design phase earns its keep. We run these numbers in the first meeting.

Additions are structural work first and finish work second, which suits us. PGX has delivered more than 150 remodels and additions over 20-plus years in South Florida, all permitted and inspected, and the hard-won lesson is that a good addition disappears: the new tie-beam carries like the old one, the stucco texture matches, the roofline looks original. We keep a written fixed scope, a daily site supervisor, and a plan for the family living in the house while the crane is in the driveway. Your neighbors on a quiet island street will judge us; we plan for that too.

faqs.q: Can I add a second story to my Key Biscayne house?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Many of the island's concrete-block homes can carry a second story once foundations are evaluated and the structure is reinforced — and building up is frequently the only way to add serious square footage without fighting lot-coverage limits. The project takes structural engineering, Village of Key Biscayne review, and High-Velocity Hurricane Zone detailing. We start with a feasibility check on your specific foundation, not a generic yes.

faqs.q: How does the FEMA substantial-improvement rule affect an addition?
faqs.a: The value of your addition counts toward FEMA's substantial-improvement threshold, which the Village enforces. If total improvements approach half your structure's market value, the whole building can be required to meet current flood-elevation standards — a major scope change. We design to the rule, not around it: the flood math happens in the first design conversation, so you choose the project's size knowing exactly what it triggers.

faqs.q: Does new construction on the island have to meet base flood elevation?
faqs.a: New habitable space in the island's flood zones generally must be built to base flood elevation requirements, which affects foundation design, floor heights, and how an addition meets the existing house. It sounds like bureaucracy, and it is also what keeps your new family room dry when a storm pushes water across the Key. We handle the elevation surveys and design details as part of the permitting package.

faqs.q: How long does a home addition take from first sketch to finished room?
faqs.a: Additions are a two-season project, honestly. Design, engineering, and Village review typically occupy the first several months; construction takes several more depending on size and whether you are adding up or out. We phase the work so your household keeps functioning, protect the occupied part of the house, and publish a schedule you can hold us to, with regular updates instead of driveway guesswork.

faqs.q: Will the addition actually match the original house?
faqs.a: That is the test of a good addition, and we treat it as a line item, not a hope. Stucco texture, roof tie-ins, window proportions, and floor levels are matched deliberately, and the structural connections are engineered so nothing telegraphs where old meets new. On streets this established, an addition that announces itself costs you twice — once to build, once at appraisal. Ours are built to disappear into the house.

outdoor-living.local_heading: Built for salt, sun, and the odd storm
intro_paragraphs: People do not move to Key Biscayne for the interiors. Life here runs outside, toward the pool, the seawall, the dock, the shaded terrace where dinner happens ten months a year. So village-core owners are replacing builder-grade patios with proper outdoor rooms, and waterfront homes from Harbor Point to Cape Florida are adding summer kitchens, pergolas, and terraces scaled for real entertaining. The catch is the environment doing the entertaining: salt air corrodes standard hardware in a season or two, so everything we specify — fasteners, framing, appliances, finishes — is chosen for a barrier island, not a catalog.

Outdoor projects are still permitted projects. The Village of Key Biscayne's Building, Zoning and Planning Department reviews structures, electrical, plumbing, and gas lines the same way it reviews interior work, and zoning rules on setbacks and lot coverage apply in the backyard too. Anything with a roof or a frame — pergolas, trellises, covered terraces — must be engineered for the High-Velocity Hurricane Zone, with anchoring designed for uplift rather than optimism. On a low-lying island, we also treat drainage as a design item: terrace elevations and slopes planned so a king tide or a summer downpour drains away from the house, not into it.

PGX approaches exteriors as one coordinated package rather than five separate trades. Terraces, stucco and paint, impact openings, re-roof coordination, and the summer kitchen all move on one schedule, under one written scope, with one supervisor on site daily, so the driveway is not a staging yard for months. We have spent more than 20 years building in South Florida, and on a small island where everyone knows everyone, we keep job sites clean, quiet, and finished on the timeline we put in writing. When the last pallet leaves, the yard should look like the renderings, minus the rendering people.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for a pergola or summer kitchen in Key Biscayne?
faqs.a: Yes. Shade structures, covered terraces, and summer kitchens involve structural anchoring, and often gas, electrical, and plumbing — all reviewed by the Village of Key Biscayne and, because this is the High-Velocity Hurricane Zone, engineered for wind uplift with approved products. Setbacks and lot coverage apply outdoors too. We fold the permitting into the project so the review happens once, correctly, before anything is built.

faqs.q: What materials actually survive the salt air out here?
faqs.a: Marine-grade ones, chosen without sentimentality. That means 316 stainless steel for hardware and grill components, powder-coated or anodized aluminum over raw steel, porcelain and dense stone for surfaces, and coastal-rated finishes on anything painted. Standard big-box hardware can start corroding within a season this close to the ocean. We specify for the environment first and the catalog second, and we tell you which choices trade longevity for looks before you make them.

faqs.q: Can you build a terrace or outdoor kitchen near my seawall?
faqs.a: Usually, with planning. Waterfront lots carry setbacks, and work near the water's edge can involve county environmental review on top of the Village permit — something we identify during design rather than discover during construction. We also engineer drainage carefully at the seawall line, since that is where grade, tide, and runoff all meet. The result is a terrace that enjoys the water without picking a fight with it.

faqs.q: Will a new terrace make my drainage or flooding worse?
faqs.a: Not if it is designed as drainage first and paving second. On a low island, every hardscape project changes where water goes, so we plan elevations, slopes, and drains so runoff moves away from the house and toward proper collection — and we think about king tides, not just average afternoons. Done carelessly, a beautiful terrace becomes a shallow reflecting pool every October. Ours are built to stay dry underfoot.

faqs.q: What does a full outdoor living project cost?
faqs.a: Scope drives it more than square footage: a paver terrace is one budget, while a covered outdoor room with a summer kitchen, gas, and engineered shade is another entirely. Marine-grade materials cost more up front and repay it by not dissolving. We price the whole exterior as one written scope — terrace, kitchen, structures, lighting — so you approve a single coordinated number instead of five contractors' worth of surprises.

Because most of the island sits in a FEMA flood zone, the Village also applies the substantial-improvement rule, and work at a seawall or dock adds county environmental review on top.

PGX Builders Group is a licensed general contractor, not a permit broker. We file our own work, coordinate the engineer or architect when a project needs drawings or calculations, and meet the inspector on site instead of leaving you to explain the job. That means a written scope before anything is submitted, a supervisor here daily so inspections get called at the right stage, and no shortcuts offered even when someone asks for one. Twenty-plus years in South Florida and more than 150 remodels and additions, every one permitted and inspected, taught us the cheap way through plan review is the expensive way out.
permitting-compliance.scope_heading: The compliance work, start to sign-off
permitting-compliance.scope_intro: Some of this is planning ahead. Some of it is cleaning up what a previous owner left behind. We do both in writing, before anyone touches the house.

scope_items.name: Permit applications and plan review
scope_items.desc: Drawings assembled, Village contractor registration current, submittal filed — then every plan-review comment answered until the permit is actually in hand.

scope_items.name: Closing out open permits
scope_items.desc: We pull the property's permit history, work out what each open record still needs — a final inspection, a revision, a permit after the fact — and get it signed off.

scope_items.name: Product approvals and anchorage
scope_items.desc: Windows, doors, and roofing specified with Miami-Dade approved products, approval documents filed with the submittal, because the inspector asks for paperwork before glass.

scope_items.name: Inspections, called in order
scope_items.desc: Phased inspections scheduled at the right stage with the work genuinely ready, so the trade behind it is not idling on the island waiting for a re-inspection.

scope_items.name: Milestone inspection repairs
scope_items.desc: For island condo buildings, we price and build the structural, waterproofing, and electrical repairs an engineer's recertification or milestone report calls for.

faqs.q: There is an open permit on my Key Biscayne house from the previous owner. What now?
faqs.a: It is solvable, and much easier before a closing date than after one. We pull the permit history from the Village, read what each open record is missing, and sort it: some need only a final inspection, some need a revision or an engineer's letter, and work done with no permit may have to be permitted after the fact and opened up for inspection. The Village closes a permit by inspecting it, so this is real work, not a phone call.

faqs.q: Who issues building permits on Key Biscayne, the Village or Miami-Dade County?
faqs.a: The Village of Key Biscayne runs its own Building, Zoning and Planning Department, so residential permits are filed, reviewed, and inspected by the Village rather than by the county. Contractors must be registered with the Village before an application is accepted, and plans move through the Village's online review. Miami-Dade still appears in two places: the product approvals required in the High-Velocity Hurricane Zone, and county environmental review for seawalls, docks, and other work in the water.

faqs.q: Does my remodel need a permit if we are not moving any walls?
faqs.a: Almost certainly. Permits follow the trade, not the drama. Electrical, plumbing, mechanical, window and door replacement, roofing, water heaters, and most of what happens behind a wall are permitted and inspected work even when the floor plan never changes. Paint and a cabinet swap generally are not. The rule we give owners is simple: if a licensed trade is doing it, assume a permit, and let us confirm before the crew arrives rather than after a neighbor calls it in.

faqs.q: Our condo building received a recertification or milestone inspection report. Can you do the repairs?
faqs.a: Yes, and that is the right division of labor. The report comes from a Florida-registered engineer or architect the association hires; we are not that professional and will not pretend to be. We take on the repair scope it produces — concrete restoration, waterproofing, railing and balcony work, electrical corrections — permitted through the Village, inspected, then handed back to your engineer for the follow-up report. In buildings like Key Colony and Ocean Club, we schedule around residents rather than the crew.

faqs.q: How much does permitting add, and how long does plan review take?
faqs.a: Permitting is part of the cost of building legally, so it goes in the written scope instead of surfacing later. Fees are set by the Village and scale with the value of the work, so we quote them against your real scope rather than guess at a number here. Timing is honest: plan review on a serious project runs in weeks, not days, and longer when the drawings are thin. The fastest permit is a complete submittal, and that is where we spend the effort.
